newsitem.title: UK: Dollar flags against yen, euro shares weaker.
newsitem.headline: Dollar flags against yen, euro shares weaker.

text.p: The dollar ended almost two yen lower in Europe on Thursday and extended its decline this month to almost 10 percent as heightened speculation of a rise in Japanese interest rates hit global currency markets.
European shares, meanwhile, ended mostly down.

In currencies, the prospect of a rise in Japanese rates is prompting investors who extensively used cheap yen borrowings to fund high-yield, high-risk currency positions around the world -- so called carry trades -- to pare back their riskier investments.

"At the end of the day, what we're seeing is a sharp rethink of carry trades in risk markets which has been triggered by the sudden shift in Japanese interest rate expectations," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"The collapse in dollar/yen itself has been exaggerated by the argument both Japan and the U.S. have engineered a stronger yen to offset the pressures that are building for a rate rise."

The dollar slumped to as low as 114.70 yen in early trade from 117.95 late on Wednesday and although it recovered some lost ground through the session it still ended sharply down at 116.28. The dollar also weakened briefly against the mark although it closed the day slightly higher at 1.6986 compared with 1.6974 late on Wednesday.
The yen surge overnight was exaggerated by a rumour that U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin favoured the dollar settling back to about 115 yen.
Traders contacted could not source the story but volatile markets needed only the slightest excuse to buy yen.
"It's become a cat-and-mouse game where the yen rallies because rates could rise, but the more the yen rallies the less likely a rate rise is," said a trader at a U.S. bank in London.

And there is still a degree of uncertainty about whether the U.S. Federal Reserve will lift interest rates at its policy-making meeting next week. The chance of another quarter-point rise in the Fed funds rate has buoyed dollar/mark.
European shares finished mostly weaker having started weaker on Wall Street's disappointing overnight close, then remaining under pressure when Wall Street opened down.

In London, shares finished slightly lower as some investors decided to lock in profits ahead of next Tuesday's U.S. Federal Reserve monetary meeting -- deliberations which could prompt a near-term rise in U.S. interest rates.
The FTSE 100 index closed 5.7 points lower at 4,681.2. Dealers said British blue chips could see more near-term profit-taking following the FTSE's month-long, 10 percent rally.

"This market is still due for a correction. Tomorrow people will start worrying about a Fed rate hike," one senior dealer said. "Wall Street is looking a bit wobbly and is also due for a correction. I would certainly look to sell into any rally."
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped around 30 points in its first few minutes of trade on Thursday following stronger-than-expected U.S. consumer price data.

Core inflation, or consumer prices ex food and energy, rose 0.3 percent against a 0.2 percent consensus forecast, raising fears that the Fed will push up its key short-term funds rate after Tuesday's FOMC meeting.

"The overall tone of the numbers is disappointing. The rise in the core rate has shifted the pendulum in favour of the Fed tightening. But it's still a close call," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist with DKB International.
U.S. blue chips turned moderately higher by the 1530 GMT London close, however, helping to lift the FTSE off its session low point of 4,654.4.
"There was nothing exciting about the figures and the trading statement didn't exactly set the market on fire," one market maker said.
German shares were dominated by the dollar's movements as the market searched for fresh fundamental data to support another run at record levels, traders said.
"The DAX index is rising and falling with the dollar," said one Frankfurt trader.
The DAX index, prompted by the dollar trading below 1.69 marks, fell 11.58 points to 3,562.11 points, while the IBIS DAX extended the drop to 3,557.88 points.
French shares edged up to a fresh closing record, however, helped by a positive reaction in the U.S. financial markets to inflation and other economic data.

The blue-chip CAC-40 index closed up 1.38 points, or 0.05 percent, at 2,776.01, surpassing Wednesday's closing record of 2,774.63 after erasing its early losses. Gold prices slipped briefly up during the afternon after German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said his country would not sell a single ounce of gold.
Gold closed in London at $346.95 per ounce, down $1.70 from Wednesday after a bounce of less than a dollar immediately after Waigel's statement.
Reports of possible German gold sales surfaced overnight and knocked about $2.00 per ounce off bullion in New York.
Germany was forecast to face a budget deficit of around 18 billion marks in 1997. Revaluing its gold reserves would be one way of plugging the gap.
STOCK PRICES CLOSING PRICES
London's FTSE 100 ended down 5.7 points at 4,681.2.
The Paris CAC-40 index ended up 1.38 points at 2,776.01.
Frankfurt's DAX index ended down 11.58 points at 3,562.11.
CURRENCIES AT EUROPEAN CLOSE
The dollar stood at 1.6986 marks in late trade compared with 1.6977 on Wednesday and 116.28 yen versus 118.83.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold ended at $346.95 after closing at $348.65 an ounce in London on Wednesday.
